blocks.text: How can we prove properties about infinitely many objects, especially when each depends on several others? Enter strong and structural induction.

blocks.markdown: Induction is a powerful tool in mathematics for proving statements about an infinite set of objects. While ordinary induction works well for sequences where each term depends only on its predecessor, strong induction is useful when each term may depend on several preceding terms. Structural induction, on the other hand, is used for proving properties of recursively defined structures.

blocks.title: Strong Induction
blocks.text: Strong induction is a proof technique where, to prove a statement for all natural numbers, we assume it is true for all numbers less than a given number and then prove it for that number.

blocks.markdown:
The principle of strong induction can be formally stated as follows: To prove a statement $P(n)$ for all natural numbers $n$, it suffices to show:
1. Base Case: $P(0)$ is true.
2. Inductive Step: For any $k \geq 0$, if $P(0), P(1), \ldots, P(k)$ are true, then $P(k+1)$ is true.

blocks.title: Example of Strong Induction
blocks.prompt: Prove that every integer greater than 1 is a product of prime numbers.

steps.text: Base Case: For $n = 2$, 2 is a prime number, so the statement holds.
Inductive Step: Assume the statement is true for all integers from 2 to $k$. Consider $k+1$.

If $k+1$ is prime, it is a product of itself. If not, it can be written as a product of two integers, both greater than 1 and less than $k+1$. By the inductive hypothesis, both are products of primes.
Thus, $k+1$ is a product of prime numbers.

blocks.answer: By strong induction, every integer greater than 1 is a product of prime numbers.

blocks.title: Structural Induction
blocks.text: Structural induction is a proof technique used to prove properties of recursively defined structures, such as trees or lists.

blocks.markdown: To use structural induction, we prove that a property holds for the base case of the structure and that if it holds for the components of a structure, it holds for the structure itself.

blocks.title: Example of Structural Induction
blocks.prompt: Prove that the number of leaves in a full binary tree is one more than the number of internal nodes.

steps.text: Base Case: A single node tree (a leaf) has 1 leaf and 0 internal nodes. The property holds as $1 = 0 + 1$.
Inductive Step: Assume the property holds for all full binary trees with $k$ internal nodes.
Consider a tree with $k+1$ internal nodes. It can be formed by adding two children to a leaf of a tree with $k$ internal nodes.
The original tree had $k+1$ leaves and $k$ internal nodes. Adding two children converts one leaf to an internal node and adds two leaves, resulting in $k+2$ leaves and $k+1$ internal nodes.
Thus, the property holds for $k+1$ internal nodes as $k+2 = (k+1) + 1$.

blocks.answer: By structural induction, the number of leaves in a full binary tree is one more than the number of internal nodes.

rows: Assume for components, prove for structure
blocks.caption: Comparison of Induction Types

blocks.title: Choosing the Right Induction
blocks.text: Use strong induction when each case depends on multiple previous cases. Use structural induction for recursively defined structures.

points: Strong induction assumes all smaller cases to prove the next case.
Structural induction is used for recursively defined structures.
Choosing the correct induction method depends on the problem structure.
